articles.title: How does Anthropic make money? Inside the business of AI.
articles.summary: Usage fees, subscriptions, and cloud sales drive revenue for AI companies, but computing costs cut into profits. Learn how AI companies make money — and if t...
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

AI companies make money mostly through subscriptions and model usage, and some also sell ads.

According to the IPO filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Anthropic, the creator of Claude, earned $33.24 billion in revenue in the first nine months of 2026. About 79% of that came from usage fees paid by developers and businesses, and 21% came from subscriptions. Revenue is not profit: Anthropic reported a $1.26 billion operating loss over the same nine-month period, driven largely by high computing costs.

Anthropic (ANT) , which began trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT, opened at $111.50 per share on Nov. 19. The company's IPO filing gives us a rare look at how an AI company makes money and where that money goes.

If you're considering investing in Anthropic or other AI companies, it's worth understanding how these companies earn money and what they spend it on.

AI companies earn revenue by charging for access to their models or selling ads. The mix each company uses depends on who they're selling to and how customers use the service. Money raised from investors funds the business, but it doesn't count as revenue.

Customers pay a monthly fee for more features or higher usage limits than the free plan offers. Claude Pro, for example, costs $20 a month when billed monthly.

A flat fee keeps your bill predictable, but it doesn't necessarily buy unlimited use. If you're a heavy AI user, you may need a pricier plan or have to pay for extra usage, which brings in more revenue for the AI company.

An application programming interface (API) lets a business connect its software to an AI model. For example, an online store can use an AI model to answer shoppers' questions. The store pays for the work the model does behind the scenes.

Text-based API bills often count tokens, which are small pieces of text. The store may pay different rates for the text it sends to the model and the answer it receives. Its choice of model, tools, and other features can also affect the bill.

For example, if an AI model charges $2 per million tokens it receives and $10 per million tokens it sends, the store would pay $12 for 1 million tokens each way. As more shoppers use the assistant, the store's usage bill grows, increasing the AI company's revenue.

3. Enterprise contracts and per-seat plans

AI companies sell workplace plans, often called enterprise plans. These plans help companies manage employee access, connections to internal tools, and security.

Businesses may pay per seat or negotiate usage charges and minimum spending commitments. Claude's Enterprise plan, for instance, combines seat fees with usage billed separately at API rates. More paid seats and usage can increase the revenue an AI company earns from each business customer.

Cloud marketplaces let businesses buy AI model usage through a cloud provider they already use. Amazon Bedrock, for example, offers models from multiple AI developers. An online store could buy model access through Amazon rather than directly from the AI developer.

Amazon then collects the payment and passes the AI developer its share. That gives the AI developer another way to earn usage revenue without handling the sale directly.

Some companies also sell ads. OpenAI, for example, has been testing Sponsored Agents, which let users chat with a business-sponsored assistant after clicking an ad.

Anthropic, on the other hand, has said it won't put ads in Claude. For companies that offer ads, payments from advertisers add a revenue stream alongside fees paid by users.

Revenue is what a company earns from customers, not what it keeps. It makes a profit only when revenue exceeds expenses. For AI companies, expenses can run high because both developing models and answering users require costly computing resources.

Generating AI answers takes substantial computing power. Each time you send a prompt, the model performs many calculations to write its answer piece by piece. That process is called inference.

Those inference computing costs grow with usage, which makes a flat monthly fee tricky for the AI company. Someone who runs coding tasks all afternoon can cost much more to serve than someone who asks for answers to a few questions, even if both pay the same subscription price.

Cheaper answers don't always mean smaller bills

More efficient chips and models can make AI cheaper to use, encouraging people to use it more. This is called the rebound effect. If that extra usage more than offsets the efficiency gains, total computing demand rises — a result known as Jevons paradox. If the cost per task drops by half while customers do four times as many tasks, total processing costs double.

Efficiency doesn't guarantee higher profits, either. Competition may push AI companies to lower their prices, passing some of the savings to customers instead of keeping them as profit.

Running today's model is only part of the costs an AI company has to balance. With competition running high, AI companies continually work to improve their flagship models by training them on larger datasets and examples. However, training requires substantial computing power and skilled staff before the model can be released to customers.

AI companies often sign long-term contracts to secure the computing power needed to train and run their models. Reserving this compute capacity helps them prepare for growth. However, these contracts typically require minimum payments that remain due even when the company is losing money.

Profitable models vs. profitable companies

A model can bring in more money than it costs to answer customers' requests. But the company still has other bills to pay, including research, staff, advertising, and business operations.

That's why covering a model's running costs doesn't guarantee a companywide profit. If total costs grow faster than revenue, profit can fall even as more customers sign up.

Companies sometimes present an adjusted profit that leaves certain expenses out of the calculation. That can turn a reported loss into a profit on paper without changing what happened in the business. Before judging how profitable an AI company is, make sure to check which costs were left out and why.

When Anthropic took steps toward going public, it filed a document called Form S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The filing shows how much money Anthropic brought in and where it came from.

Here's Anthropic's revenue breakdown for January through September 2026:

Most of Anthropic's money comes from usage, not monthly plans. Developers and businesses pay for the work Claude does, while subscriptions cover plans with included access and features.

One customer can land in both buckets. A paid Claude plan counts as subscription revenue, while extra usage bought on top of it counts as usage revenue.

Customers can buy Claude directly or through cloud marketplaces. Marketplace sales made up about 44% of revenue during the first nine months of 2026.

For those sales, Anthropic counts the full customer payment as revenue. The cloud partner's share appears separately as a sales and marketing expense, so reported revenue includes money that ends up with partners.

Anthropic brought in $33.24 billion in revenue during the first nine months of 2026, but its results look different depending on which costs you count:

Operating loss: Across the business, operating expenses totaled $34.5 billion during the nine months. That left a $1.26 billion operating loss under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP), the standard U.S. accounting rules.

Adjusted operating profit: Anthropic reported $4.08 billion after leaving out $3.26 billion in pay through shares or options and $2.09 billion tied to matching employees' charitable donations with company shares. Anthropic says the exclusions make ongoing results easier to compare. These costs don't involve cash payments, but issuing shares can reduce existing investors' ownership.

Overall net loss: Anthropic reported a $104.04 billion net loss. About $94.32 billion came from earlier financing deals, mainly loans that can turn into shares. As the company's value rose, so did what those investors were entitled to receive. Accounting rules counted that increase as an expense, although no cash was paid out for it during the period.

Computing costs: The company recorded $18.81 billion in computing and infrastructure expenses, more than half its revenue. That includes developing models and running them for customers and is already included in its operating expenses.

Future commitments: Anthropic has committed roughly $900.9 billion to future payments, nearly all for computing and infrastructure. About $70.7 billion is due in the 12 months ending Sept. 30, 2027. These are future obligations, not expenses to add to the nine-month loss.

The companies that develop AI models aren't the only ones benefiting from AI spending. Companies that supply chips, memory, and computing power can also profit from AI. And businesses can make money by building products on top of existing models.

Chipmakers such as Nvidia ( NVDA ) sell the processors used to train and run AI models. They get paid when customers buy hardware, whether or not those customers ever turn a profit.

AI processors also need fast memory working alongside them. Companies such as Micron ( MU ), SK hynix ( SKHY ), and Samsung sell specialized memory called high-bandwidth memory, or HBM.

Micron pointed to AI-driven demand as it reported a roughly 256% rise in revenue to $133.19 billion for its 2026 fiscal year, which ran from late August 2025 through early September 2026.

Cloud providers, such as Amazon ( AMZN ), Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ) , and Microsoft ( MSFT ), rent out computing capacity to AI developers like Anthropic and OpenAI. They can also earn fees when customers buy AI model usage through their marketplaces.

Many companies don't build their own models. They pay for access to someone else's and sell a product built around it, such as customer service software or a coding assistant.

These companies avoid funding the model's entire training program but instead depend on their AI supplier's prices. They still need to charge enough to cover model access and their other costs.

What to look for before investing in AI stocks

Revenue growth alone doesn't give you a complete picture of whether an AI stock is a good investment. The costs behind the revenue can cut into profits, and the expectations built into the share price can affect its future price potential.

These measures help show whether growth is turning into money the company keeps:

Revenue and run rate: Look at recent sales momentum as well as revenue already earned. Run rate stretches recent activity over a year, so it can highlight growth that a full-year total hasn't caught up with yet. Anthropic put its run-rate revenue at about $81 billion as of Oct. 31, 2026. Bringing in that amount over a full year would depend on maintaining that pace.

Margins: Track whether the company keeps more of each revenue dollar as it grows. An operating margin improving from -10% to -5% means an operating loss of 5 cents per dollar of sales instead of 10 cents, and is not an operating profit yet. Compare the same margin definition, including which costs an adjusted version leaves out.

Computing spend: Check whether computing expenses are growing faster or slower than revenue. Faster cost growth can squeeze profit. Training a new model is different from spending more to serve existing customers. Where the company provides a breakdown, separate those costs to better understand its finances.

Cash flow: Look at cash from operations alongside spending on equipment. Accounting profits don't guarantee that the business generates enough cash to fund those investments. If it uses more cash than it brings in, check how long its cash reserves could cover the gap before it needs new funding.

5 risks to keep in mind when investing in AI stock

Even with strong demand, rising costs and high expectations can make an AI investment risky.

Pricing pressure: Lower prices and heavy usage can squeeze profits even as sales grow. If earnings fall short of expectations, investors could see the share price fall.

Capacity commitments: Large fixed payments leave less room for setbacks. If cash runs short, the company may need to borrow more or sell new shares, reducing existing investors' ownership. Capacity booked for expected growth can leave it paying for resources it doesn't need if demand disappoints.

Supplier costs: Higher chip and memory prices can leave less money from sales to cover other expenses. Investors may have to wait longer for the company to turn a profit.

Partner dependence: An AI developer may rely on a cloud company that also competes with it. Losing favorable pricing or access to customers could weaken the business and the value of your investment.

High valuations: A strong business can still be a disappointing investment if you pay too much for its shares. A price built on rapid growth leaves little room for slower sales or weaker profits.

Claude brings in subscription fees and charges for usage, including access through APIs and cloud marketplaces. Most of Anthropic's revenue comes from paid usage rather than fixed subscriptions.

Not automatically. A subscription can be attractive when customers use relatively little computing capacity. Heavy usage can make it more expensive to serve. API billing ties revenue more directly to usage, but pricing, discounts, and delivery costs still determine the profit.

Anthropic reported $33.24 billion in revenue during the first nine months of 2026. That's money earned from customers before expenses, not profit. When comparing that figure with another company's sales, check that both cover the same period.

How do AI companies get paid by businesses?

Businesses can pay AI companies per employee account or buy usage through an API or cloud marketplace. A single agreement can combine seat fees with usage charges. The price may also cover administrative controls, connections to internal systems, and other features a free AI assistant doesn't provide.

Most AI developers don't publish enough financial detail to give a clear answer. Anthropic's IPO filing offers a closer look. It reported an operating loss for the first nine months of 2026, but a profit after excluding certain expenses. If you're considering investing, check what a company's profit claim leaves out and whether it reflects the whole business.

articles.title: EPFO approves SWP for PF retirees, reduces minimum balance need: How it benefits you; check calculations
articles.summary: In a significant move, the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) board on Thursday approved the provision for a Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP)
articles.body: In a significant move, the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) board on Thursday approved the provision for a Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) for retiring members. The step is being seen as a game-changer for retirement planning, allowing for members to withdraw their provident fund corpus in instalments over their lifetime, instead of as a lump sum.The aim is to provide EPF members with a dependable income after retirement, while also limiting their reinvestment risks. With an SWP, members will receive predictable payments from their retirement savings while retaining ownership of the remaining corpus and earning interest payouts on it.To begin with the move is expected to benefit approximately 6.32 lakh EPF members who are above the age of 55 years and have provident fund accumulations of over Rs 5 lakh.How will the EPF SWP work? How long will your retirement corpus last if you opt for a systematic withdrawal plan? Will it be better than other traditional investment avenues that retirees opt for? We decode:Systematic Withdrawal Plan on EPF, changes in minimum balance: Top 10 pointsThe SWP facility will allow you to choose a withdrawal frequency for your EPF corpus post retirement. You will not be mandated to withdraw it in lump sum within three years of your retirement.The frequency of SWP can be monthly, quarterly, or even half-yearly, depending on what you opt for.The balance amount of your corpus will continue to earn interest.The scheme is intended to provide a regular source of income after retirement, help members earn returns on their remaining savings and supplement their pension benefits.You don’t have to opt for the SWP, it will be voluntary.If during the payout period, an EPF member passes away, the nominee or the dependent will be allowed to withdraw the outstanding amount or even continue with the SWP.Yet another aspect would be implemented in future, which would allow for UAN-linked facilities for direct voluntary deposits and small contributions from third parties, such as customer tips. This is particularly relevant for gig workers. These transactions would operate independently of conventional employer payroll systems, providing additional flexibility and supporting the objective of universal social security.EPFO board also approved changes to the minimum balance that members must have in their EPF accounts and the waiting period for final withdrawals. Members will now be required to retain only 10% of their contributions in their accounts at all times. The waiting period for withdrawal has also been shortened from 12 months to two months.What it means for youThe move is important because most EPF members tend to withdraw their entire corpus at retirement.That can in turn expose the money to poor investment choices, family pressures or importantly, the risk of outliving savings. With an SWP, a single payout turns into a predictable income stream.Puneet Gupta, Partner, EY India explains the basic takeaway: The proposed Systematic Withdrawal Plan could give employees more choice in how they use their provident fund savings after retirement.Instead of taking the entire PF amount at one go, a member could withdraw it gradually, on a monthly, quarterly or half-yearly basis, while the balance continues to earn EPF returns.“For retirees, this could help create a regular stream of income and also reduce the need to immediately decide how to reinvest a large lump-sum amount. Since the option is voluntary, members would still have the flexibility to choose what works best for their retirement needs,” Gupta tells TOI.Vivek Iyer, Partner and Financial Services Risk Advisory Leader, Grant Thornton Bharat believes that the move fills a long-standing gap in India's retirement system, which has focused on building savings but offered little help in turning them into income.Fundamentally, it gives retirees another investment and savings avenue alongside the existing options of pension and annuity products that can generate regular post-retirement cash flows.Other benefits announced today also assume significance.Puneet Gupta tells TOI, “The reduction in the minimum PF balance requirement from 25% to 10% gives employees greater access to their PF savings through partial withdrawals for permitted needs such as housing, medical treatment and education. In practical terms, members can now access up to 90% of their PF balance, compared with 75% earlier, while retaining a smaller portion for long-term social security.”“The waiting period has also been reduced from 12 months to two months. The press release refers to this specifically in the context of final PF withdrawal. It would therefore be useful to have further clarity on whether the revised waiting period applies only to final withdrawal after cessation of employment or has any impact on partial withdrawals as well,” he adds.How SWP on your EPF account could workNow let’s take a look at a hypothetical SWP with regards to PF withdrawals. Let’s say a member retires at 58 with a Rs 50 lakh balance in his EPF account.The member decides to opt for a Rs 40,000 monthly withdrawal from his PF account. According to calculations shared by Grant Thornton Bharat, the retirement corpus will last for around 24 years, that is approximately till the age of 82 years. The payout will be around Rs 1.15 crore, because the remaining balance will keep earning interest, even as part of it is withdrawn every month.Below are some more hypothetical calculations of how long your retirement corpus of Rs 50 lakh can last at a retirement age of 58, assuming an annual interest rate of 8.25%. It’s important to note that EPFO reviews the interest rate for provident fund every year, and is therefore subject to change.As Vivek Iyer points out, subscribers need to look at inflation as the real trade off: raising payouts 5% a year protects purchasing power but shortens the plan by about four years compared with a flat Rs 40,000.According to Vivek Iyer, the nominee benefit is real: if the member dies at 68 on the Rs 40,000 plan, about Rs 39.6 lakh passes to the nominee. A typical life annuity would not return that.Also, the interest preserves the corpus. Drawing Rs 34,375 a month, which is roughly the interest earned, leaves the full Rs 50 lakh for the family.In the above two examples, it is important to note that:Interest is compounded monthly for simplicity. EPF actually calculates interest on monthly running balances and credits it once a year.Tax, charges and any changes to payout amounts are ignored.EPFO's final SWP rules, including how the remaining balance earns interest, will determine the actual outcomes.A TOI report earlier today cited calculations by EPFO that indicate that if a retiree opts for SWPs, they will actually earn more on the same amount than what annuities or even bank fixed deposits get.Kuldip Kumar, Partner at Mainstay Tax Advisors LLP says it would be important to examine the detailed framework once implemented, particularly with regard to withdrawal limits, the manner of interest accrual and the rate of interest applicable to the unwithdrawn balance.“Currently, under the existing EPF provisions, interest ceases to accrue once an account becomes an 'Inoperative Account'. Under Paragraph 72(6) of the EPF Scheme, this generally happens where a member retires after attaining the age of 55 years, migrates abroad permanently or dies, and no application for withdrawal is made within 36 months from the date the amount becomes payable,” Kumar tells TOI.A similar provision applies where an amount remitted to a member is returned undelivered and remains unclaimed for 36 months, subject to the prescribed exceptions.What does it mean for your taxes?The tax treatment is an important aspect to watch, and one that as of now doesn’t have clarity. The Labour Ministry’s release says that a corresponding amendment to the Income-tax Act for the SWP will be taken up with the Ministry of Finance.Puneet Gupta notes that currently, PF withdrawal is generally tax-exempt where an employee has completed at least five years of continuous service, subject to applicable conditions.According to Gupta, another point that will need clarity is the tax treatment of interest earned on the PF balance after retirement or cessation of employment.Under the existing tax framework, such interest may be taxable.“It will therefore be important to see whether the proposed tax changes also address the treatment of interest earned on the amount that remains with EPFO under the SWP,” Gupta tells TOI.Kuldip Kumar believes that the tax treatment - whether periodic withdrawals under the proposed SWP will enjoy the same tax-exempt treatment as an eligible lump-sum PF withdrawal on retirement - will be a key factor in determining its attractiveness and how it compares with other financial instruments offering systematic cash flows.The bottom lineExperts say the success of the new scheme will lie in its execution and finer details as and when they emerge.Vivek Iyer sums it up: If executed well, the SWP could become India's default way of drawing retirement income and set a benchmark for annuity and mutual fund providers. Above all, it treats retirement as a stream of income rather than a single payout.“Ultimately its value will depend on how the remaining balance earns, how instalments are taxed, and how flexible the plan is,” he concludes.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: US, India working towards 'fair, reciprocal' trade ties, says US Embassy Deputy Chief
articles.summary: US Embassy Deputy Chief of Mission Jason Meeks on Thursday said that New Delhi and Washington are working closely to build a trade relationship that is
articles.body: US Embassy Deputy Chief of Mission Jason Meeks on Thursday said that New Delhi and Washington are working closely to build a trade relationship that is "fair, reciprocal and mutually beneficial."Speaking at the 23rd India-US Economic Summit, Meeks said that cooperation between both countries reaches well beyond the trade of goods."We've made real progress, and our progress reaches well beyond trading goods. Our two nations are partnering on energy, on pharmaceuticals, on critical minerals, on advanced technology, and on manufacturing," Meeks said.During his address, Meeks also described the Pax Silica Declaration - signed between both countries - as "a landmark agreement that makes it easier for American and Indian companies to work together across borders."The deputy chief of mission also said that the pact would empower the next generation of entrepreneurs and builders in both countries to bring new ideas to market.He added that the United States, India and other countries signed the "San Francisco Declaration" just a few days ago to strengthen the Pax Silica framework.Meeks also underlined the importance of resilient supply chains and said, "Supply chain resilience is not just an abstract policy goal, although it sometimes sounds like one. When disruption hits, whether from a pandemic, whether from a conflict or from a natural disaster, American and Indian industries must be able to adapt together, diversify together, and keep production moving forward.""From automotive components to pharmaceuticals to electronics, Indian firms are becoming an essential link in our global supply chains," he said, adding that American companies are bringing "the technology, the capital, and the know-how" that help those chains grow stronger.On trade, Meeks stressed that "fair market access helps both ways." He said the two governments should create an environment where American suppliers and technology can "freely reach Indian manufacturers and consumers", and where Indian firms can "compete fairly in US markets.""When trade is fair and reciprocal, workers and companies on both sides win," he said.Pointing to the scope for deeper engagement, he said, "There's still a lot of potential to unlock. As we keep reducing barriers to trade and working together in every field, we will build a future that is free, open, resilient, and prosperous for us all."Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: K’taka GCCs  account for 43% of India’s AI talent: Report
articles.summary: Karnataka hosts 43% of India’s GCC AI talent and nearly half of AI/ML CoEs, led by Bengaluru, says Zinnov-KDEM report on 1,088 GCCs.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Karnataka’s GCCs are moving AI forward, with their global mandates increasingly centred on engineering, product development and ownership.The state accounts for 43% of India’s GCC AI/ML workforce and nearly half of its dedicated AI/ML centres of excellence (CoEs), according to a report by Zinnov in collaboration with the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM).The report estimates that Karnataka has 1,088 GCCs, accounting for 51% of India’s 2,117 centres. These include 320 of the 506 GCCs set up by Global 2000 companies. The centres employ more than 829,000 people, including 111,000 AI/ML professionals and 414,000 engineering research and development (ER&D) professionals.Between FY21 and FY26, Karnataka attracted 217 of the 510 new GCCs established in India, accounting for 43% of the additions. It also accounted for 46 of the 89 new Global 2000 centres and 55 of the 102 new GCCs set up by companies headquartered on the US West Coast.Karnataka IT minister Priyank Kharge said the report demonstrated the maturity of Karnataka’s GCC ecosystem. “The state’s overall AI/ML capabilities and AI maturity are 1.12 times the national average. We intend to ensure that this becomes at least twice the national average by next year,” he said at the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026 on Thursday.Kharge said that while the government, venture capital firms, incubators and colleges were contributing to the ecosystem, GCCs themselves were nurturing more than 5,500 technology startups. More than 5,000 investors had invested in startups in the state. “Karnataka’s share of India’s AI startups has risen to 29%, while its share of the country’s incubators and accelerators stands at 15.4%,” he said.The study found that 69% of Karnataka GCCs have dedicated AI budgets, against 57% nationally. An equal proportion conduct role-specific AI training, compared with 53% nationally. About 83% reuse in-house AI platforms across business units, against 57% nationally, while 66% follow Responsible AI practices, compared with 49% nationally.Karnataka has 451,000 professionals across emerging technology skills, including AI, data science, cloud, cybersecurity and robotics. It also has 60,000 of India’s 110,000 technical engineering leaders, or 55% of the total.Bengaluru accounts for 44% of India’s senior AI leadership job postings in GCCs. Demand for senior AI talent in the city is 6.4 times the average of other tier-I cities, rising to 14.2 times for distinguished and principal AI engineers. The city accounts for 63% of such specialised postings nationally.The share of Bengaluru GCC job postings seeking AI skills rose from 8.5% in 2024 to 13.6% in 2026, compared with 9.8% at the same companies’ offices outside Karnataka. Recruitment is increasingly seeking skills in generative AI and agentic frameworks such as LangGraph, LangChain, prompt engineering and model evaluation, alongside observability, MLOps and platform engineering.More than 660 GCCs in Karnataka have AI/ML capabilities, while the state hosts over 120 dedicated AI/ML CoEs. These account for nearly 48% of India’s 250-plus such centres, about four times the number in the next-largest hub. About one in three of these CoEs has a generative AI or agentic AI mandate.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? Join the TOI Money Masterclass.

articles.title: K’taka, Amagi sign LoI to set up sports technology CoE in B’luru
articles.summary: Karnataka signs LoI with Amagi to set up a govt-backed Sports Technology CoE in Bengaluru, focusing on sports analytics, biomechanics and athlete development.
articles.body: Bengaluru: The Karnataka govt has signed a Letter of Intent (LoI) with Amagi Media Labs to set up a Sports Technology Centre of Excellence (CoE) in Bengaluru, envisaged as India’s first govt-backed centre dedicated to sports technology.The proposed centre will bring together technology, research and industry expertise to strengthen the state’s sporting ecosystem and promote the use of technology in athlete development and sports performance.Karnataka IT minister Priyank Kharge said the sports ecosystem, valued at around $41 billion, is expected to grow by 12-15% in the coming years, presenting an opportunity for Karnataka.The centre will focus on three areas: core technology and research, athlete development, and ecosystem enablers. Its research areas will include sports analytics, deep tech, biomechanics, health and life sciences, and sports hardware and electronics.The athlete development vertical will cover simulation and virtual training, injury prevention and rehabilitation, athlete well-being and psychology, talent identification, assistive technology, women in sports, coaching and capacity building. The third pillar will focus on applied research, testing and validation, skilling, and collaboration between institutions and industry.The state govt will provide seed funding and facilitate infrastructure, while the centre will be professionally managed. “It will be run by the industry, for the industry and for the sports fraternity,” Kharge said, describing it as a unique experiment for the country.Karnataka has experience in setting up industry-partnered CoEs, with more than 20 centres in the state, including C-CAMP, Bengaluru Bioinnovation Centre, ARTPARK and CISEC. articles.title: Senate Republicans resist Trump’s bid to bypass Democrats on defense funding
articles.summary: Senate Republicans are pausing President Donald Trump’s request to pass $350 billion in defense funding through a party-line bill to attempt to negotiate a d...
articles.body:
Senate Republicans are pausing President Donald Trump's request to pass $350 billion in defense funding through a party-line bill to attempt to negotiate a deal with Democrats after facing midterm backlash over the Iran war.

"We want to explore all the possibilities for funding the military, one of which would be seeing whether or not there's an appetite on the Democrat side to do it," Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) told reporters Wednesday after meeting with Senate Republicans. "I don't know that they will. But we think that we ought to at least explore that possibility."

Though Republicans will first attempt to negotiate a deal with Democrats, both Thune and Senate Budget Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wisconsin) said that a party-line bill is not completely off the table.

Thune's announcement came after multiple meetings over the past week where GOP senators discussed Trump's $350 billion request and whether Republicans could come to a consensus. However, passing yet another party-line bill drew concerns from multiple Republicans.

"I'm not for a partisan Republican bill to spend more money or borrow more money," Sen. Rand Paul (R-Kentucky) said Wednesday. "There's quite a few of them that I guess did not, were not aware of what happened with the election recently. All the exit polling showed that people were upset about the price of gas and the Iran war."

Republicans control the Senate 53-47, meaning they cannot afford to lose more than three votes on a party-line bill if every senator is voting. And the party's margin is set to shrink Dec. 15, when the term of Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) - who was appointed last year to fill Vice President JD Vance's Senate seat - expires.

Republicans are grappling with how to handle Trump's request to fund the Pentagon as they reckon with crushing midterm losses that cost them control of both chambers, in part due to voters' negative sentiment toward the war with Iran.

Some Republicans lined up behind Trump's renewed call last week for Republicans to go it alone on defense funding, as Democrats have been opposed to sending any money to the Pentagon that could be used toward the war.

"I think we have a responsibility when people protect us to keep them safe, just like they're keeping us safe," Sen. John Boozman (R-Arkansas) told reporters Wednesday. "And if you leave them underfunded, then that creates a huge problem for the people who serve."

articles.title: GTA 6: Made in Bengaluru, set in Miami
articles.summary: GTA 6 launches set in Vice City (Miami), with over 1,600 developers at Rockstar’s Bengaluru studio contributing; Newzoo projects $4.5B launch-week sales.
articles.body: Bengaluru: The first thing that strikes you when you boot up GTA 6 is how good Vice City looks, right down to the neon reflected in a convertible’s windscreen.Grand Theft Auto VI, the action-adventure game developed and published by Rockstar Games, is set in a fictional city modelled on Miami. But part of the game took shape much closer to home. More than 1,600 developers at Rockstar’s Bengaluru studio worked on it, Bengaluru South MP Tejasvi Surya said on X on the eve of its release.In July, games researcher Newzoo projected that Grand Theft Auto VI could generate $4.5 billion in worldwide sales by the end of its launch week, including pre-orders. When the game arrived on Thursday, players had waited 13 years for a sequel to GTA V, which had sold nearly 235 million copies.Some of the details that bring Vice City to life require painstaking research. Rockstar developers travelled to Miami and visited nightclubs to study their lighting. Aaron Garbut, one of the game’s development leads, told Bloomberg that the team had to work out what each patron would do, animate those movements and make the lights change in sync with the music.Rockstar has said little about which parts of Vice City its Bengaluru team worked on. But the city’s contribution to the game has roots in a local studio whose recruits once spent their first two weeks playing video games at work.Rajesh Rao, founder of Dhruva Interactive, started a multimedia business in Bengaluru in 1995 and moved into game development in 1997. Many of his early hires, he recalled, had never even seen a gaming console.Joshi Mark Premnath, a founding member of Dhruva, recalled on LinkedIn how the team visited British Library to study picture books and sketch from them. Its engineers also figured out how to render three-dimensional scenes on a Pentium PC without a separate graphics accelerator.In November 1998, Dhruva won a contract to develop a PC version of Mission: Impossible. The publisher eventually shelved the project, leaving the developers with a game they could demonstrate to prospective clients but one that never went on sale.At a game developers’ conference in 2001, Rao spotted Microsoft’s Ed Fries on a street corner and stopped him to demonstrate the game on his laptop. At a subsequent meeting with Microsoft, Dhruva showcased cars its artists had modelled for British games company Codemasters. Microsoft had just approved a racing game called Forza Motorsport.Studios on Microsoft’s shortlist were given four weeks to build four cars. Each had to look convincing up close, show damage after a crash and have a simpler model for when it appeared in the distance. Dhruva’s artists used the same tools as their counterparts at Microsoft, and both teams reviewed the work. “Since then we’ve worked on every Forza that’s ever been built,” Rao said in 2017.By 2016-17, overseas studios were sending Dhruva rough layouts of game levels and relying on its team to turn them into detailed environments that players could explore. When Rockstar acquired Dhruva in 2019, about 300 employees joined its Bengaluru studio. Rockstar already had around 500 employees in the city.There is an interesting parallel between the work on Vice City’s nightclubs and one of Dhruva’s early demonstrations for American publishers. Years before Rockstar’s developers travelled to Miami to study its clubs, Dhruva had built a bar of its own to showcase its capabilities. It was a Wild West saloon after closing time, with the barman cleaning up.The idea, Rao told Thomas Friedman for his book The World Is Flat, was to give prospective clients a piece of their own culture to judge the studio’s work. Nobody on the Bengaluru team had ever set foot in a real saloon.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? Join the TOI Money Masterclass.

articles.title: 24 VCs announce Rs 1,050 cr investments in deeptech startups
articles.summary: 24 VCs announced Rs 1,050 crore in deeptech startup investments at Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026, led by Accel, 3one4 Capital and Gaja Capital.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Twenty-four venture capital firms announced investments worth Rs 1,050 crore in deeptech startups at Bengaluru Tech Summit on Thursday, with three investors accounting for over 70% of the total. Karnataka IT minister Priyank Kharge said the announcements covered more than 68 startups.The investments were unveiled at Future Makers Conclave on the summit’s concluding day. An investor-wise schedule showed Accel accounting for Rs 321.3 crore, 3one4 Capital Rs 228.2 crore and Gaja Capital Rs 200 crore. Together, their allocations came to Rs 749 crore, or about 71% of the total.Accel’s listed investees included Ajna Aerospace & Defence, Alt Inc, Chaos Engine Labs and Dreamteam AI. The 3one4 Capital allocation covered companies including Sunfox Technology, Neufin, Fernbox and Green Aero, while Gaja Capital’s investment was linked to QNu Labs, which develops quantum-security technology.Other announced amounts included Rs 44 crore from Merak Ventures, Rs 35.95 crore from Avana Capital, Rs 30.7 crore from Arali Ventures, Rs 27.5 crore from Ideaspring Capital and Rs 24.5 crore from Speciale Invest. The beneficiaries ranged from robotics and aerospace ventures to companies working on semiconductors, artificial intelligence and biotechnology.The figures represent investment announcements, not necessarily funds already transferred to startups. The event document did not specify how much of the total had previously been committed or when individual investments would be deployed.Kharge said the commitments had been put together in less than a month. When organisers met two or three weeks earlier, the amount being discussed was around Rs 600 crore, he said. The final figure crossed Rs 1,000 crore through the efforts of participating investors and industry bodies.“Now show me one state in India which is capable of delivering on a government stage across sectors, across 24 venture capital firms, 1000 crores in less than one month,” Kharge said.He also said Karnataka’s startup ecosystem had crossed $4.4 billion in funding this year, accounting for 43% of technology investments in India, according to figures cited by him.The conclave also marked 10 years of Elevate, Karnataka’s grant programme for early-stage ventures. An event presentation said the scheme had committed Rs 393.58 crore in grants and helped generate more than 6,500 jobs.Sharath Bachegowda, chairman of Keonics, said Elevate funding did not require founders to surrender equity. BioAI Innovations founder Shilpa Nargund said receiving the grant helped her company win investor confidence after some backers suggested setting up the business overseas. She said the biotech startup subsequently raised nearly $1 million in equity funding.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? Join the TOI Money Masterclass.

articles.title: Data gaps, skills shortage slow AI adoption in India’s aerospace sector: Report
articles.summary: Report: AI adoption in India’s aerospace, defence and space sector is slowed by data gaps, high costs, procurement hurdles and a shortage of “digital engineers.”
articles.body: BENGALURU: Artificial intelligence adoption across India’s aerospace, defence and space industries remains uneven, with fragmented data, high technology costs, procurement hurdles and a shortage of specialised engineers limiting its wider use, according to a new industry report.The report, Intelligent by Design: AI Adoption in India’s Aerospace, Defence & Space Industry, prepared by TiE Bangalore and the Aerospace India Association (AIA), found that while some global engineering centres in India were already using AI in production, several traditional design and manufacturing companies continued to depend largely on conventional automation.The findings are based on interviews, working sessions and written contributions from industry executives, engineers, suppliers and founders between August and early November 2026. The report cautioned that these accounts were not a representative survey of the entire industry.One retired design head from a defence public-sector enterprise reported that AI had not been used in his design division during his tenure, although former colleagues had subsequently begun exploring its applications. In contrast, an Indian engineering centre of a global aerospace manufacturer reported using AI across business functions, with separate teams overseeing research, deployment and governance.The report identified four recurring challenges: fragmented and restricted access to data, commercial terms that discourage adoption, a shortage of engineers combining domain knowledge with AI expertise, and uncertainty over how to assess the capabilities of AI systems.Procurement emerged as a particular concern. Some contributors described situations where technologies considered proven had failed to secure repeat orders. Long procurement cycles, payment terms and the absence of follow-on contracts made it difficult for technology suppliers to justify further investment.The report said AI could help manufacturers predict quality defects, improve production schedules, interpret complex engineering requirements and identify potential supply-chain disruptions. In aircraft maintenance, applications included predicting equipment failures, forecasting spare-parts requirements and analysing maintenance records.However, it cautioned against treating every proposed application or pilot as evidence of commercial adoption. AI-assisted designs would also continue to require verification and certification, particularly for safety-critical aviation systems.A major recommendation emerging from the analysis was the need to develop what the report called the “digital engineer” — a professional trained in a core engineering discipline who could also apply AI to practical industry problems.It argued that classroom training alone was insufficient and that engineers needed to demonstrate their abilities through actual projects.The report set a goal of making AI an operating advantage for India’s aerospace, defence and space industries by 2030, helping improve engineering capabilities, production reliability and the country’s ability to secure more complex global manufacturing work.It also called attention to the need for greater coordination among industry, academic institutions and policymakers, particularly around data access, procurement and workforce development.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Trump Sold Home Depot, McDonald’s as Portfolio Shifted to ETFs
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s sprawling investment portfolio shifted into dividend-producing ETFs and government securities in September, selling blue-chip names...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump's sprawling investment portfolio shifted into dividend-producing ETFs and government securities in September, selling blue-chip names like McDonald's Corp., Home Depot Inc., and Comcast Corp.

Trump's September trading report, released Thursday by the Office of Government Ethics, showed that he bought nearly 100 municipal bonds worth at least $18 million in the first half of September, most of them maturing within two years. His biggest single transaction of the month was a purchase of the Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF that cost between $5 million and $25 million.

The portfolio's biggest moves into short-term bond index funds coincided with a broad market selloff on Sept. 23 that pushed five-year yields over 5%.

Trump has defied precedent by maintaining an active portfolio while in office, trading more stocks and bonds in his second term than every member of Congress combined — even as he's called for a ban on congressional stock trading that would exempt the president.

Trump has said he doesn't manage the portfolio day-to-day, but relies on third-party financial institutions trading using automated strategies that track broad market indexes.

The latest disclosures show that the president's biggest muni bond purchases, for at least $1 million each, were for debt financing a Northern Kentucky sewer district, Pittsburgh hospitals, a San Antonio community college, an Orlando redevelopment district and two affordable housing projects. He's also a creditor to Yale University and to the authority behind Houston's professional sports stadiums.

At the same time, the September report showed the president was a net seller of a wide range of individual companies, decreasing his positions in Nike Inc., Constellation Brands Inc., and Fidelity National Information Services Inc. But he continued to buy stock in big-name tech companies, with incremental purchases in Netflix Inc., Nvidia Corp., Oracle Corp., Tesla Inc., Amazon.com Inc. and Apple Inc.

Among the largest stock picks in September was TJX Companies Inc., owner of off-price retailers TJ Maxx and Marshalls. His net position in that company increased somewhere between $251,000 and $964,000. Officials are only required to list the size of their transactions within broad ranges on the disclosure forms.

articles.title: Anthropic starts trading in the US after blockbuster IPO
articles.summary: Anthropic’s IPO surpasses SpaceX, marking the largest initial public offering in US history at $81bn.
articles.body:
Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI assistant, is now trading on the Nasdaq through the largest initial public offering in history, surpassing the debut of Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

The stock began trading on the ticker ANT midday on Thursday.

The artificial intelligence (AI) lab, valued at $2 trillion, said last week that it would offer 825 million shares with its initial public offering (IPO) at a price range of $70 to $78 per share. However, that changed on Wednesday when the Dario Amodei-led company announced it would sell 980 million shares at $83 each.

By the time the stock ultimately went live, at 11:50am in New York (16:50 GMT), it was trading at $111.50 per share, a 34 percent rise. It dipped below $100 in midday trading, hitting $95.69 by 1:55pm (18:55 GMT).

The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down 1.5 percent in midday trading, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average is down by 1.8 percent and the S&P 500 is down 1.5 percent.

Other tech giants are also trending downwards, with Microsoft down 1 percent, Nvidia tumbling 1.7 percent, Meta down 2.5 percent, Apple by 0.9 percent, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) by 9.2 percent and Micron Technology by 0.5 percent.

The high-profile IPO has fuelled excitement across the board, including among industry insiders such as Michael Monaghan, founder and portfolio manager at Founders ETF.

“We have indicated our intention to buy in the IPO and hope to get an allocation. The books are well oversubscribed with high-quality orders, according to our trading counterparts,” he told Al Jazeera.

Anthropic’s listing is the first of the two major AI labs to go public on US markets, as competitor OpenAI has also eyed an IPO. However, it comes at a rocky time for the AI industry, amid the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia invested a combined $20bn in Anthropic, including $10bn in a partnership announced in November 2025 and another $10bn in a share purchase tied to its IPO.

The massive IPO also comes amid backlash from voters in the recently concluded midterm elections, where all but one ballot initiative restricted expansion of data centres, and a sweep by Democrats who ran on platforms of reining in the AI industry.

“Some of the demand may simply reflect investors not wanting to miss out on the rare opportunity to gain exposure to a leading AI company, even if its long-term profitability remains uncertain,” IPOX associate Lukas Muehlbauer told the Reuters news agency.

That has not dented analysts’ assessments of the sector.

“Anthropic’s IPO [is] a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning,” Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director of Yorkville Ives, said in a note.

Anthropic is also closely watched for how intertwined it is with other tech companies, including Amazon and Google.

Anthropic has committed $110bn to Amazon for computing infrastructure over long-term agreements and at least $121.3bn to Google.

Anthropic’s Wall Street debut comes amid growing concerns about the safety of its technology. The company’s more than 300-page US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing devoted approximately 90 pages to outlining potential risks, including warnings that its AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”.

The company also disclosed a net loss of $104bn in the first nine months of 2026 in its SEC filing.

The concerns come as a group of AI safety experts has criticised Anthropic in a new statement released in the days surrounding its IPO. Dubbed the “Misanthropic Statement”, it challenges the company’s claims about its commitment to developing safe AI.

“Anthropic is not a safe AI company, and we must reject its reckless attempt to amass power in the name of the greater good,” the statement said.

Amid the concerns, the company put out a lengthy statement on the social media platform X.

“We will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” the statement quoted Anthropic CEO Amodei as saying. “We will not bend to either business or political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing.”

articles.title: How the FAA Ground Stop Could Cost Airlines $1 Billion — and Why the Economic Toll May Be Higher
articles.summary: The FAA ground stop not only cost the airline industry billions, but created lost revenues across the U.S. Here are the financial ramifications so far.
articles.body:
U.S. Transportation Secretary, Sean Duffy, stated in a briefing on November 16 that the airlines faced between $345 million and over $1 billion in losses as a result of the FAA's November 13 ground stop which brought air traffic to a screeching halt.

According to FlightAware data via Reuters , 18,500 flights "flying within, into or out of the United States" to be canceled as of Monday morning. That's roughly 18% of all scheduled air traffic between Friday and Monday.

While investigations into the exact cause are still underway, one thing is clear: the damage is far-reaching. Duffy stated the broader U.S. economy lost "billions of dollars" from the 4-hour fiasco.

The financial impact reached far beyond the airline industry however, and may result in more losses as events, hotels, restaurants and more report the impact.

Keep reading to learn what the cost of the ground stop is so far.

According to the U.S. Department of Transportation , airlines must issue full cash refunds to consumers when airlines cancel or significantly delay flights if passengers "choose not to travel or accept travel credits, vouchers or other forms of compensation offered by the airline."

Airlines are also forced to refund checked baggage fees, seat selection fees and any boarding upgrades previously purchased.

Because the ground stop and the cascading cancellations happened on a Friday, passengers missed inflexible weekend events for which many could not re-book: weddings, reunions, sports games, concerts, etc, which means they did not rebook flights and simply took the refund.

In addition to not being able to move passengers, flight crews and planes were also displaced and had to be transported outside of regularly scheduled flights to continue service.

For example, if a flight attendant was scheduled to work a flight from Atlanta to Chicago and that flight was cancelled, the flight attendant would be unable to work her next scheduled flight from Chicago to Dallas.

Once the ground stop was lifted, flight attendents were "deadheaded" to their proper locations. AeroCorner explained that deadheading means flying pilots and flight crews as passengers to their designated locations—resulting in additional compensation, hotel accommodations, food vouchers and shuttle services for the affected crew.

Additionally, the Wall Street Journal reported that, once work resumed, airlines paid overtime to flight crews, pilots and maintenance workers in order to clear the backlog.

articles.title: AMD stock drops after Hunterbrook Media raises export control concerns
articles.summary: Hunterbrook Media has raised questions about AMD's exposure to US export controls related to China.
articles.body:
AMD ( AMD ) stock plunged more than 8% on Thursday after Hunterbrook Media published an investigation raising questions about potential export-control issues related to the chipmaker's products.

Hunterbrook Media is associated with Hunterbrook Capital, which has a short position on AMD.

According to the outlet , Chinese server maker IEIT continued to receive firmware updates for AMD's chips, despite being blacklisted by the US Department of Commerce.

Hunterbrook also claims three companies associated with IEIT, but not blacklisted, used software virtually identical to the firmware used by IEIT.

AMD, however, refuted Hunterbrook's claims in a statement to Yahoo Finance.

"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," a company spokesperson wrote.

"AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."

AMD rival Nvidia ( NVDA ) has also faced scrutiny over former CEO Jensen Huang's alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy and over concerns that customers circumvented export controls by shipping chips to China.

Huang resigned from Nvidia late last week and was replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress.

AMD is viewed as a potential beneficiary of Nvidia's stumbles.

The company's stock is up more than 110% over the past 12 months, while Nvidia shares are down as much as 18%.

The AI trade has faced a number of headwinds recently as investors question the stability of the AI build-out and whether the boom will continue at its current pace.

articles.title: Anthropic stock's first trade was worth $12 billion — 34% above its IPO price
articles.summary: The biggest IPO ever opened 34% above its offer price in a $12 billion first trade.
articles.body:
Wall Street waited until nearly noon for Anthropic's first trade. That one print was worth about $12 billion.

Anthropic ( ANT ) opened Thursday at $111.50 a share, 34% above its $83 IPO price, as 108 million shares changed hands in the opening trade. That single print was bigger than SpaceX's ( SPCX ) entire first minute of trading in June, about $9 billion.

The first full minute was bigger still. About 139 million shares, roughly $15 billion of stock, traded in Anthropic's first 60 seconds, by Yahoo Finance calculations. That's nearly twice SpaceX's first minute, about three times Alibaba's ( BABA ) in 2014, and about 14% of the 980 million shares sold in the offering.

The rush capped the biggest IPO ever. Anthropic raised $81.3 billion after pricing above its $70-$78 range , and the opening price valued the company at nearly $2 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

The 34% opening pop was about three times SpaceX's 11%, though well short of Cerebras' ( CBRS ) 89% in May. IPOs priced above their marketed range have averaged a 50% first-day gain since 1980 , according to data from University of Florida professor Jay Ritter.

Plenty of people are already richer. Existing shareholders paid an average of $11.50 a share, so the open came in at almost 10 times their cost. And Wall Street's banks are sharing about $550 million in fees .

IPO buyers stand to gain the most on day one. Every $1 that Anthropic closes above $83 adds nearly $1 billion to the money left on the table — the gap between the IPO price and the first close, times the shares sold. A close above about $98 would top SpaceX's $14.4 billion, the most on Jay Ritter's list of US IPOs since 1985 , by Yahoo Finance calculations.

The first trade is often the high point.

All 12 of the biggest US IPOs since 2008 fell below their first trade within a year . SpaceX opened at $150 in June and closed at $143.50 on Nov. 18.

NYU Stern professor Aswath Damodaran valued Anthropic at $76 a share in a Nov. 18 blog post , before the IPO was priced. He wrote that "the real comparison should be to the price that Anthropic will open trading at tomorrow." The opening trade came in more than 45% above his number.

"The most difficult work lies ahead of us," CEO Dario Amodei said Thursday.

articles.title: The outages keep coming. Some Americans are preparing for a collapse.
articles.summary: Canning fruits was a hobby for Korrie Roth until Microsoft Outlook went down. And then the planes stopped flying. And then Apple Pay froze up. And then the N...
articles.body:
Canning fruits was a hobby for Korrie Roth until Microsoft Outlook went down. And then the planes stopped flying. And then Apple Pay froze up. And then the National Security Agency, whose responsibilities include defending the government from cyberattacks, reported its own mysterious outage.

"Now I'm prepping for survival," said Roth, a 37-year-old IT specialist and mother of five, who lives in Greenwood, Indiana.

No explanation from the country's leaders has soothed her.

President Donald Trump suggesting everything is "fine" on Tuesday lacked empathy, she thought. She was not feeling fine, and her social media feeds were full of panicked friends asking some version of: What is going on?

"You're supposed to trust the government to give you information and protect you," she said. "But we are worried, and the government is just like, 'Oh, you're silly.'"

Roth bought a crank radio and extra bottled water and checked in with someone she actually trusts right now - her father. He bought a portable generator during the Microsoft crash, he told her.

A slew of seemingly unrelated outages, coupled with media reports both vague and menacing, have led to a groundswell of worry from Americans who said they're preparing for a bevy of worst-case scenarios: Widespread power outages? Electrical grid failure? The end of the world?

The political response has offered little clarity. Some Republicans have amplified suspicions that the outages are connected. "The American people can see everything happening with these service outages, and they feel like they're not getting the whole story," Sen. Rick Scott (R-Florida) wrote Tuesday on X, demanding transparency from companies and federal agencies.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) was more pointed. "If this is all a coincidence, it's like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world," he told reporters at the Capitol.

The administration, by contrast, has sought to tamp down speculation. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday he understood why people are nervous but the government had "zero evidence" linking the outages. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee in a Wednesday hearing that while Americans are right to ask questions, "these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack."

But on the internet, where "preppers" are sharing tips on Facebook groups and Reddit communities, nothing seems outside the realm of possibility - especially to people who have long maintained that they're prepared for anything.

articles.title: Trump administration makes it easier for companies to classify workers as contractors
articles.summary: Nov 19 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump's administration unveiled a final rule on Thursday that will make it easier for companies in some industries to...
articles.body:
Nov 19 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump's administration unveiled a final rule on Thursday that will make it easier for companies in some industries to classify workers as ‌independent contractors rather than their employees, who have more legal protections and can cost more.

The ‌Department of Labor scrapped a rule adopted during the administration of former President Joe Biden, a Democrat, and replaced it with a legal ​test favored by business groups.

The new rule could lower costs for companies in a range of industries, including trucking, healthcare, retail sales and app-based transportation and delivery services such as Uber, that rely heavily on contractors. Such companies routinely face lawsuits accusing them of misclassifying workers to save money, which they deny.

The Labor Department said the ‌2024 rule was legally flawed and ⁠that the new test creates a clearer standard for businesses and workers to follow.

"It's more important than ever to ensure our labor regulations keep pace with the changing ⁠ways that Americans choose to work, and businesses choose to operate," Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said in a statement.

The rule will take effect in January, 60 days after it is formally published.

The Biden-era rule ​had ​established factors for determining whether a worker should be ​classified as an employee or contractor under federal ‌wage law, and any one of them could tip the scales toward employee status.

The rule finalized on Thursday instead focuses on whether workers are under a company's control or have the opportunity for profit or loss based on their own initiative or investment.

Employees can cost businesses up to 30% more, according to several surveys, because they are entitled to the minimum wage, overtime pay, unemployment insurance, reimbursements for expenses and ‌other protections not afforded to contractors.

Worker classification has been one ​of the most contentious employment-related issues over the last decade, and ​trade groups lobbied heavily to repeal the ​2024 rule after an effort by Republicans in Congress to block it stalled.

The Biden-era ‌rule had replaced a regulation adopted during Trump's ​first term that said ​workers who own their own businesses or can work for competing companies — such as a driver who works for Uber and Lyft — can be treated as contractors. The new rule is similar ​to that standard.

Supporters of the Biden-era ‌rule have said misclassification of workers is rampant in some industries, and that repealing the rule ​would allow employers to strip workers of basic legal protections.

(Reporting by Daniel Wiessner in Albany, ​New York, Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi and Rod Nickel)

Influential investor Keith Gill, also known as Roaring Kitty, has returned, and GameStop ( GME ) shares are rising after the meme stock trader who made millions betting on the company returned to the discourse as gamers everywhere celebrated the release of "Grand Theft Auto VI."

After being MIA online for nearly two years, at 11:30 a.m. ET on Thursday, Roaring Kitty tested the waters with a mysterious post on X: a photo of "Cat Mario."

GameStop stock popped roughly 3% immediately following his tweet.

Gill's post lands at a dizzying moment for markets, just roughly an hour after Anthropic's ( ANT ) IPO went live and on the day Take-Two ( TTWO ) launched GTA VI.

Yesterday, GameStop CEO Ryan Cohen said publishers are making a mistake by releasing games as digital downloads instead of physical discs. "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend," Cohen told Bloomberg .

GameStop's stock is up more than 30% since the beginning of the year, buoyed by its eBay ( EBAY ) stake and interest .

The image is of Mario wearing a cat power-up in "Super Mario 3D World." It's not clear what Roaring Kitty's Mario post means — if anything at all — but the market is reacting and powering up the stock.

articles.title: Walmart, Costco see some panic-buying after tech outages
articles.summary: Outages at Apple, Chase, Microsoft, and US airlines could mean good news for Walmart.
articles.body:
A wave of tech outages and disruptions affecting Apple ( AAPL ), Chase ( JPM ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), and US airlines has sent consumers spiraling over the past week, prompting people to stock up on emergency supplies.

"We have seen a small amount of that," Walmart ( WMT ) CFO John David Rainey told Yahoo Finance (see video above). "Certainly categories like jug bottled water or propane are selling at higher comps with that concern, but it's really relatively small to our overall business. It's worth noting that oftentimes when we see that, it's a pull forward of future demand."

Rainey said the company will stick to its outlook despite a minimal sales lift. On Thursday, Walmart raised its full-year outlook for the third time this year. It now expects net sales to increase by 4.9% to 5.2%, up from 4% to 5%.

Walmart isn't alone in seeing panic buying amid consumer anxieties that a cyberattack or other outage could lead to more catastrophic system failures. Wholesale retailer Costco ( COST ) is also seeing a boost, according to Mizuho analyst David Bellinger.

"Consumer anxiety, following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media, have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at Costco," he wrote in a note to clients.

As of Nov. 15, he said 21 of the 26 high-ticket generators online were sold out.

"These one-time lifts, combined with pantry-loading and a value connotation into the holiday period, all add to an already very elevated valuation for shares," Bellinger said, who raised his price target on Costco stock to $1,150 from $1,110.

Shoppers stockpiling emergency supplies led to an increase in same-store sales growth at US Costco stores, not including fuel purchases. Sales increased 11% to 12% in the final week of October, Bellinger wrote, adding that the bump continued in the first two weeks of November.

Search "doomsday food" on the Costco app, and shoppers will find that emergency food supplies from ReadyWise , Ready Project , and Chef's Banquet are all sold out.

Yahoo Finance also reached out to Target ( TGT ) about whether it's seeing any panic buying, but the retailer said it has nothing to share at the moment.

articles.title: Kalshi hired its GTA VI 'researcher' after receiving 30,000 applications
articles.summary: Getting paid to play video games and talk about them is a real job.
articles.body:
It was the type of job posting that didn't look real. Kalshi, the prediction market, was looking for a "GTA VI researcher," someone to livestream their playthrough of Take-Two's ( TTWO ) blockbuster title, with an eye for studying the game's economy.

"This is a real job," is how the job description began.

Ahead of the game's midnight launch Thursday , Kalshi announced its newest hire, the winner of this wild sweepstakes. He goes by Cliff Savage, a recording artist, streamer, and content creator, who will now add playing GTA VI to his resume.

Kalshi's co-founder and CEO Tarek Mansour said in a post on X that Savage stood out for his work ethic and his passion for the game. Savage has nearly 16,000 monthly listeners on Spotify and more than 2,000 followers on Twitch.

Mansour's announcement also noted that Kalshi received over 33,000 applications, a staggering number that highlights the intense interest around GTA VI and the idea of getting paid to play video games and talk about them.

Besides showcasing the interest, the moment was a snapshot of the modern AI-powered labor market. Perhaps even thousands of these applications were AI-generated. But almost certainly, they were AI-screened too, as employees and employers fight fire with fire.

While we may not see these same numbers, 100 applications to a single role isn't uncommon, and getting your resume to a human is becoming a success of its own.

And now, Savage will be a human in this computer world, streaming his misadventures through a fictionalized Miami while producing weekly reports on the game's jobs, systems of commerce, and ways to build wealth.

Savage said he wants to take a frugal approach to exploring Leonida, the hyper-real, over-the-top portrayal of the state of Florida.

"I'm studying the economy before I spend a dollar," he said in a post on X. "Checking property prices, businesses, side hustles, and every possible way to make money. I want to figure out how Leonida's economy works, find the fastest path to wealth, and turn my discoveries into content my viewers can actually learn from."

Ashton Kutcher celebrated Anthropic's ( ANT ) blockbuster IPO on Thursday, and with good reason: Sound Ventures, the venture capital firm Kutcher co-founded, made a $435 million investment in Anthropic that's now worth roughly $7 billion.

"People usually see the one deal and think that's the whole thing, but the ones who know realize that it's years of work, micro victories and failures stacked on top of one another," Kutcher wrote on X.

"Kind of cool when that works out," Kutcher added.

Kutcher began Sound Ventures with Guy Oseary, a talent manager for stars like Madonna, 11 years ago. The firm was the successor to Kutcher and Oseary's first VC firm, A-Grade Investments, which was founded in 2010.

The group began investing in Anthropic in 2023 and later built up a 0.5% stake in the Claude creator.

"I see [Dario Amodei] no different than one of the greatest musicians who's got all of these ideas in their minds, and they're going to go in the studio and make an incredible album," Oseary told Bloomberg in a recent interview . "This might be one of the greatest debut albums of all time."

articles.summary: A majority of Americans support targeted tariffs on foreign steel, according to new data. Seven in 10 of the respondents to the Harris Poll survey, obtained exclusively by The Hill, said targeted tariffs should be part of the federal government’s approach to maintaining strong domestic steel production capability. About 8 in 10 Republicans and 6…
articles.body:
A majority of Americans support targeted tariffs on foreign steel, according to new data.

Seven in 10 of the respondents to the Harris Poll survey, obtained exclusively by The Hill, said targeted tariffs should be part of the federal government’s approach to maintaining strong domestic steel production capability.

About 8 in 10 Republicans and 6 in 10 Democrats backed targeted tariffs on steel imports, per the survey.

President Trump imposed tariffs on steel imports during his first term, under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 — which allows the president to tax imported goods on national security grounds.

Former President Biden maintained those levies , and Trump increased them from 10 percent to 50 percent in the early months of his second term.

The president has also threatened to slap 50 percent tariffs on Canadian imported cars, trucks, auto parts and steel starting on Jan. 1 amid his trade war with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Scott Paul, the president of the Alliance for American Manufacturing, said the need for the federal government to protect the domestic steel industry “transcends partisan politics.”

“Congress must recognize that targeted steel trade measures not only have broad bipartisan public support but are essential as American workers and manufacturers continue to fight rampant unfair trade and global overcapacity,” Paul said in a release announcing the results of the Harris Poll survey.

Roxanne Brown, the president of United Steelworkers International, also said “strategically placed tariffs” must be part of the federal government’s approach to allow domestic industries “to compete on a level playing field.”

The Harris Poll conducted its survey from Nov. 5-7, polling 1,802 registered voters. The overall results had a margin of error of 2.8 percentage points.

Democrats this midterm cycle campaigned on reining in Trump’s tariff authorities , as the levies contributed to elevated costs for Americans.

Roughly 6 in 10 respondents to a recent Reuters survey said they want Congress — which Democrats will control come January — to repeal the president’s import levies .

articles.title: Fed’s Jefferson says AI build-out ‘exerting upward pressure’ on inflation
articles.summary: Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said Thursday the artificial intelligence build-out is putting “upward pressure” on prices, while adding the technology could lower prices in the future by boosting productivity. During an International Monetary Fund and Central Bank of Brazil conference, Jefferson said AI is “likely to automate some tasks and augment others” in…
articles.body:
Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said Thursday the artificial intelligence build-out is putting “upward pressure” on prices , while adding the technology could lower prices in the future by boosting productivity.

During an International Monetary Fund and Central Bank of Brazil conference, Jefferson said AI is “ likely to automate some tasks and augment others” in the long term.

“Currently, the AI build-out is exerting upward pressure on demand and inflation,” the Fed vice chair said.

“In the future, advancements in productivity could exert downward pressure on inflation while continuing to support growth,” he added.

Jefferson also noted energy price shocks from the nearly nine-month Iran war are contributing to inflation. While gas prices are down relative to a month ago, the average price of a gallon of regular gas is roughly 63 cents higher than it was a year ago, AAA reported Thursday .

Energy prices increased by 0.7 percent from September to October, after rising by 5.2 percent from August to September, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

The increase in energy prices in the early months of the war contributed to overall inflation rising, as annual inflation remains above the Fed’s 2 percent target rate.

To combat persistent inflation , officials on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raised interest rates by a quarter point in September. In late October, the FOMC held rates steady at a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent.

While Jefferson did not forecast his vote at the FOMC’s next meeting, set for Dec. 8-9, he warned about inflation risks “becoming unanchored.”

If that occurs, he argued a “stronger reaction” from the central bank is “warranted.”

Traders are pricing in a 96.4 percent chance of FOMC officials raising rates by a quarter point next month, according to the CME FedWatch tool .
