articles.title: Anthropic passed the IPO test. Now comes the hard part.
articles.summary: If Anthropic’s first day of trading was a test, it would have passed with flying colors.
articles.body: If Anthropic’s first day of trading was a test, it would have passed with flying colors. With a $2 trillion debut at market open, the AI giant has clearly convinced Wall Street it can transform the way people work – and turn a massive profit doing it. Now comes the hard part. Anthropic will have to prove its Claude AI agent will continue to grow at a breakneck pace against the backdrop of skyrocketing computing costs and increased competition. Meanwhile, some of the businesses that have fueled its rise are starting to slow their AI spending, says one economist who monitors AI enterprise spending. As a public company, Anthropic will face even more pressure to grow each quarter. The world’s largest publicly traded AI companies – Nvidia, Google and Amazon – have seen their shares stumble even when their quarterly numbers fall in line with Wall Street’s expectations. The billions being spent on infrastructure, along with the rapid development of AI models and growing adoption among consumers and businesses, have set sky-high expectations across the industry. Anthropic investors will be looking for massive sales growth each quarter to offset the nearly trillion-dollar computing expenses the company expects to pay in the years ahead. “It’s not easy,” said Ken Mahoney, president of financial planning firm Mahoney Asset Management who closely follows the tech industry. “You go from hardly any scrutiny to everything you do, there’s an analyst revaluating.” ‘A very sticky business’ Anthropic’s early bet on building AI tools for businesses has made it a darling of the AI market. That set the stage for the company to make a record-breaking debut; it began trading at $111.50, a 34% jump from its IPO price, and closed 17% higher at $97.17 a share. Businesses are spending on AI at a rapid clip; the enterprise AI market grew fourfold in just a year from $33 billion in 2025 to $177 billion in 2026, according to Menlo Ventures, a venture capital firm that has invested billions in Anthropic and backed early-stage companies building with Claude. Anthropic’s revenue reached $17 billion in the third quarter of 2026, signaling a roughly twelvefold year-over-year increase, the company said in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. It has roughly 14,000 customers, about 250 of which contribute $10 million or more in revenue on a yearly basis. The company’s Claude Code agent emerged as an early favorite among software engineers, and Anthropic swiftly sought to replicate that success with its Claude Cowork service focused on office work. More customers have adopted Claude Cowork eight months after it was released early access, compared to Claude Code in a similar time period after its launch, Anthropic said.” Once a business is hooked on Anthropic’s products, it’ll be hard to convince them to switch, said Lauren Cassidy, chief investment officer of Founder ETFs. “They’re going to just continue to embed them in more and more applications, and that makes it a very sticky business,” Cassidy said. Can it keep growing? The big question now is whether Anthropic can sustain and boost its growth. Unlike its biggest competitors, Anthropic lacks a strong presence in the consumer AI market. Claude monthly active users have grown enormously compared to Meta AI, Google Gemini and ChatGPT. But OpenAI’s app, Claude’s most direct rival, still has a much larger pool of users, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. ChatGPT has 1.4 billion monthly active users, the firm said, compared to Claude’s 124 million. ChatGPT also beats Claude on time spent per week and in-app spending, likely an indication that ChatGPT users are increasingly paying for subscriptions, said Abe Yousef, a senior analyst for SensorTower. That may not be a big deal today. But if Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s ChatGPT increasingly become the main place people spend their day, will that eventually lead them to using it more for work? The competition is also likely to accelerate. OpenAI, expected to go public next year, is currently Anthropic’s biggest challenger. It accounts for about 40% of AI spending among American businesses compared with Anthropic’s nearly 45% according to Ramp. Enterprise spending on AI, while growing, is also very concentrated within the tech and finance industries, according to Ara Kharazian, lead economist at AI finance company Ramp. That’s a mixed bag for Anthropic; it means there’s plenty of room to expand Claude’s reach, but also that Anthropic’s business could depend on spending trends among a relatively small group of companies. The tech and finance companies that have been shelling out for AI are already starting to pull back their spending, Kharazian said. OpenAI has recently cut prices of some of its to remain competitive with Anthropic and other rivals. And some companies are turning to open models that allow businesses to more cheaply build AI agents that can run on their own hardware, which could be more secure for processing sensitive data. Oracle and other companies offer services that allow businesses to orchestrate various AI services through one platform, according to Cassidy. The system might use Claude Cowork for one query related to managing files but Grok for another that requires an answer pulled from social media. “Then the market share gets diversified away from Claude exclusively, and it gets spread where the model is also trying to optimize for cost,” Cassidy said. Claude Code helped make Anthropic an enterprise juggernaut. Now, the pressure is on Anthropic and other tech giants to figure out what comes next. “The coding agents powered this growth,” Kharazian said. “And we kind of need to figure out what the next front is going to be.”

articles.body:
Van Hollen backs populism in challenge to Schumer

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) is challenging Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) for the top spot in the Senate Democratic Caucus, and he is doing so by outlining his progressive economic positions .

Van Hollen, who is seeking to end Schumer’s nearly 10-year stint leading Senate Democrats, has taken a firm stance on regulating cryptocurrency and addressing wealth inequality .

The Maryland Democrat has also strongly criticized the role of billionaires and super PACs in U.S. elections, saying earlier this month that wealthy donors “tried to buy” the midterm elections — which saw Democrats sweep to control of Congress.

“I’ve had a record of doing what our candidates on the campaign trail talked about. A populist message of un-rigging an economic system stacked in favor of the very wealthy and fueled by political corruption,” he told Dana Bash on CNN’s “State of the Union” over the weekend.

The differences between Van Hollen and Schumer are also clear in which Senate Democrats are backing them.

The challenger has the support of economic populists such as Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), along with Sens.-elect Abdul El Sayed (D-Mich.) and Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.).

The longtime Democratic leader, meanwhile, has the moderate wing of the caucus on his side. Schumer has insisted he has the votes to remain the Senate Democratic leader, with the caucus-wide election set for Dec. 1 .

If Van Hollen wins, oversight of Big Tech is likely to be a focus for the Senate Democratic Caucus.

The Maryland senator backed bipartisan legislation aimed at cracking down on anticompetitive behavior by large technology firms during an event in California this week, Semafor reported Thursday.

Schumer, at the time the Senate Majority Leader, did not bring the legislation to the floor in 2022, arguing it did not have the 60 votes needed to avoid a filibuster.

articles.title: The world is experiencing ‘GTA VI’ together — players and spectators alike
articles.summary: Millions of people around the world are playing “Grand Theft Auto VI.” Millions more are watching other people play it.
articles.body: Millions of people around the world are playing “Grand Theft Auto VI.” Millions more are watching other people play it. Playing the blockbuster video game is mostly a solitary pursuit. But this week’s global launch has felt like a communal experience because so many gamers had been waiting so long to play. Thursday’s launch shattered live-streaming records on Twitch and YouTube. Brands seized on the frenzy with “GTA VI”-themed promotions and discounts. News outlets published live blogs to keep up with all the reactions. The game’s launch became a rare moment of monoculture in an increasingly fragmented media environment, with story after story about people skipping school or calling out sick from work to start the missions. Already, “GTA VI” has made an estimated $1.8 billion in revenue, making it one of the decade’s biggest entertainment spectacles. On release day, people collectively spent more than 132 million hours watching “GTA VI” livestreams across Twitch, YouTube and Kick, according to data from the live-streaming analytics platform Streams Charts. At one point, nearly 8 million people were watching various streams at the same time. For many fans — including those who couldn’t get out of work to play right away — watching their favorite streamers discover the ins and outs of the game has become almost as much of an event as playing it themselves. Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick, meanwhile, celebrated the Rockstar Games developers who had spent more than a decade perfecting the game. “This is a massive creative achievement on the part of Rockstar, and third parties agree with that,” he said, citing the game’s aggregate score of 99 out of 100 on Metacritic. Speaking on the TBPN podcast, Zelnick said “pre-orders were far in excess of expectations” and hinted that the company would share more about the game’s commercial performance soon. In the meantime, “Rockstar is feeling like rockstars,” as The Hollywood Reporter remarked. “GTA VI” has lived up to sky-high expectations, with reviewers praising the cinematic storytelling, deeply immersive open-world gameplay and sharp social satire. And in a week when other major companies dealt with digital disruptions, Sony PlayStation and Microsoft Xbox’s systems did not register any major outages. Neither did the platforms hosting the thousands upon thousands of live streams. It was all good, clean fun. Well, maybe not clean. This is “Grand Theft Auto,” after all. The title refers to a real-world crime. The violence is graphic, and the language is explicit. But there’s much more to the game than just mayhem. Players can lose themselves in countless everyday activities, from exploring the fictional streets of Vice City to caring for pets, working out in the gym and completing household chores. In one early mission, players have to fix a kitchen sink. Nevertheless, some Fox News commentators sounded alarms about the game’s violent content on Thursday. “I do worry about this effect on a young generation,” Kayleigh McEnany said during a midday talk show. The on-screen chyron read at one point: “AMERICANS CELEBRATE VIDEO GAME PROMOTING CRIME.” Meanwhile, some of the more online corners of MAGA complained that the game isn’t nearly as depraved as its predecessors — supposedly the result of a “woke” sanitization. Even some government agencies joined in on the hype on Thursday. “Can’t talk right now. Birdwatching in GTA VI,” the Interior Department wrote on X, referring to the fact that the game features 62 types of birds. In Miami, the real-world inspiration for the game’s fictional Vice City, the Heat took the court Wednesday night in special “GTA VI”-themed uniforms. Fans purchased the exclusive jerseys, which sold out within 90 minutes. More than 20% of ticket buyers lived over 250 miles away, Axios reported. Food delivery companies sought to capitalize on the occasion, too. DoorDash said it detected a spike in late-night energy drink orders around the launch, while Uber Eats announced fast-food deals designed “with one-handed eating in mind” — for players unwilling to put down their controllers long enough to eat. Some reviewers who were lucky enough to play ahead of launch day said they spent more than 100 hours exploring the virtual environment, and still had lots more to discover. That’s why “GTA VI” will be a cultural force to be reckoned with for years to come. Rockstar hasn’t even said when the online mode will launch. But Thursday was the start of it all, with players forking over $80 or more for digital downloads. Broadband providers like Spectrum said they detected unusually high network traffic as the title was pre-loaded onto millions of consoles. Behind the scenes, streaming platforms had also been preparing for this launch for a while. “Our engineering and operations teams have been planning for this moment for months,” a Twitch spokesperson told CNN, citing the millions of fans who would “tune in to watch their favorite creators to experience ‘GTA VI’ for the first time.” In one day, “GTA VI” has surpassed big-name games like “League of Legends” and “Fortnite” to become the most-watched gaming category in Twitch history, based on peak concurrent viewership.

articles.title: Almost all of Anthropic’s employees are now millionaires
articles.summary: Anthropic’s stock market debut turned the vast majority of the young startup’s staff into overnight millionaires — some many times over.
articles.body: Anthropic’s stock market debut turned the vast majority of the young startup’s staff into overnight millionaires — some many times over. The company’s headcount stood at 5,300 as of September this year, according to regulatory filings. After Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, about 600 employees entered the rarefied “centi-millionaire” club, with equity holdings valued north of $100 million, according to data from Hill.com, which tracks private-company shares. As many as 2,800 staffers, known internally as “Ants,” have holdings valued above $10 million. And about 5,100 — 96% of the staff — are sitting on equity north of $1 million. “What’s most surprising here is how quickly this this happened,” Andrew Benson, Hill’s founder and CEO, told CNN on Thursday, noting Anthropic has seen very little attrition. “It’s been pretty clear for some time that Anthropic is a rocket ship, and so it definitely discouraged people from leaving because they knew what the opportunity cost of that would be.” It’s not unusual for Silicon Valley startups, which are typically light on cash, to pay their staff with a combination of salary and stock. The promise of a future acquisition or initial public offering tends to keep workers motivated to work hard and stick it out until payday. But few startups have grown as big or as quickly as Anthropic. The company, founded in 2021, had fewer than 1,000 employees at the end of 2024. As with most tech startups, Benson noted, “being early is more important, in terms of a financial outcome, than being senior … You could be very low on the totem pole, and if you joined in 2023 or 2024, you’re likely to have a significantly better outcome than a senior person who joined earlier this year.” SpaceX, by contrast, spent more than two decades as a private company before its blockbuster IPO in June. That debut minted around 4,400 millionaires, out of a staff of 22,000. Anthropic’s IPO is also unique for allowing non-founder insiders to cash out on Day One of trading. In most IPOs, staff are subject to a “lockup” period — typically three to six months — during which they can’t sell their shares. But Anthropic’s listing included a complex, staggered lockup schedule that allowed non-founder insiders to cash out up to 10% of their shares as soon as the stock began trading. (It’s not known how many insiders may have taken advantage of the opportunity Thursday.) And unlike SpaceX, which has employees spread across Texas, California and Florida, Anthropic is uniquely concentrated in San Francisco, a city whose entire economy has been reshaped by sudden surges of tech wealth. A rash of newly minted millionaires could soon amplify pressure on San Francisco’s housing market, where home prices are already rising at their fastest pace in years. The typical home there sold for $1.7 million in October, up nearly 19% from a year earlier, according to Redfin. By contrast, the national median home price was roughly flat over the same period, at $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors.

articles.title: Walmart stocks up on inflation-weary shoppers ahead of the holidays
articles.summary: Walmart raised its sales outlook and reported gaining market share as it lures more affluent shoppers who are hunting for deals amid high inflation.
articles.body: Walmart isn’t just adding inventory for the holiday shopping season; it’s also racking up more customers looking for discounts as inflation maintains its grip on the U.S. economy. The retail giant on Thursday said it gained market share and raised its sales outlook for the third time this year as bargain hunters across income levels hit stores and fill their online shopping carts. “Looking ahead, we expect a strong holiday season,” CEO John Furner said on an earnings call with analysts Thursday. Walmart, which is generally considered a barometer for the U.S. economy, has long been a go-to store for consumers seeking discounts. Rising prices have pushed many consumers to rethink where they shop, and Walmart has benefited from more higher-income shoppers. As it draws more affluent customers, the company has launched a fashion-forward women’s apparel brand and expanded its e-commerce and advertising businesses. Walmart isn’t alone in gaining momentum with thrifty shoppers ahead of the holidays. Rivals Target and Costco are also seeing customers respond to their value offerings, both posting sales increases and Target raising its outlook. The results illustrate the resilience of American consumers, who keep spending even while grocery and gas prices rise and paycheck growth lags the pace of inflation. “In spite of that, consumers are finding ways to get what they need for their families,” Matthew Shay, president of the National Retail Federation, told NBC News on Wednesday. Still, it’s shaping up to be a strong holiday season, and not just for Walmart. The National Retail Federation forecasts that sales in November and December will top $1 trillion in the U.S. for the first time. But that doesn’t necessarily mean consumers are buying more items; rather, they’re paying a higher price at checkout. This season, Walmart said it lowered the price of 7,700 items by the end of the third quarter while expanding deals on groceries. The company said it will also offer a Thanksgiving meal basket for 10 at $3.50 per person, including turkey, Stove Top stuffing, mashed potatoes and other staples. Walmart also raked in more revenue from its membership fees, which surged 17% in the quarter. The company announced a bundled deal that includes memberships to Walmart+ and its warehouse-club subsidiary Sam’s Club, as well as perks including free access to streaming platforms and gas savings. While shoppers seem to be sold on Walmart heading into the holidays, Wall Street was a bit more cautious. The company’s stock slipped about 1% to $126 a share amid a broader market sell-off Thursday, even as quarterly revenue and profit surpassed investors’ expectations. Goldman Sachs analysts said they still rated Walmart’s stock a “buy,” projecting it’ll hit $132 a share. Nonetheless, they also flagged risks to the company’s outlook, including the potential for an economic slowdown and more intense price competition from its big-box and online rivals.

articles.title: Irdai flags conflict in banks, auto companies selling insurance
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Irdai chairman Ajay Seth has called for stronger corporate governance in the insurance sector, citing potential conflicts of interest when lenders
articles.body: MUMBAI: Irdai chairman Ajay Seth has called for stronger corporate governance in the insurance sector, citing potential conflicts of interest when lenders sell insurance and automobile dealers combine insurance distribution with vehicle repair services.He also called for boards to act as the first gatekeepers of governance, drawing on RBI's engagement with bank and NBFC boards. Separately, he questioned whether financial regulators should erect barriers between sectors or allow savings to move towards more efficient managers, while flagging risks from the widespread use of AI in insurance underwriting and claims settlement.Speaking at the Gatekeepers of Governance 2026 event in Mumbai helmed by former Sebi chief M Damodaran, Seth said business models that had served the industry for decades could also create conflicts of interest. He said boards needed to establish safeguards to ensure these conflicts did not compromise customer interests."Some business models have served very well over decades, but that brings in the associated risks in terms of conflict of interest," Seth said. Citing lenders selling insurance and automobile dealers combining insurance distribution with damage repair services, he said, "These are the two different signs of services. They have to be kept separately rather than mixing with each other."Seth said boards had a responsibility to establish safeguards against such conflicts. "The role of the board becomes more important, that what kind of a guardrail it sets to take care that those conflicts of interest do not come in the way of providing the best advice, best service, best product to the customers," he said.He also called for the insurance sector to strengthen corporate governance by adopting practices followed by RBI in its engagement with banks and NBFCs. He cited RBI's structured interactions with company boards and independent directors as an approach that had helped improve governance across the financial sector.On the movement of household savings between financial products, Seth questioned whether regulators should create barriers between sectors or facilitate the flow of savings towards more efficient managers. He said changing preferences were reshaping the way savings were managed and called for greater coordination among financial regulators.Seth also flagged the risks arising from the growing application of artificial intelligence tools in the insurance sector.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Piyush Goyal calls for trusted supply chains between India & US
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal on Thursday called for building resilient and trusted supply chains between India and the US amid
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal on Thursday called for building resilient and trusted supply chains between India and the US amid prevailing global uncertainties. This helps countries reduce dependence on one geography, securing supplies of critical goods and strengthening India-US economic and strategic ties, the minister said.Addressing the Indo-US Economic Summit here, he said huge potential exists between the two countries to enhance economic cooperation, as the US offers capital, technology, and innovation, while India offers skills, talent, manufacturing strength, and competitiveness. Goyal said he would conclude with five calls to action, using the acronym TRUST to outline his suggestions."T - the first letter. Let us turn our supply chains into resilient and trusted supply chains. 'R', let us raise our talent together with our friendly and partner countries," he said. The minister suggested increasing collaborations between Indian and US universities. "I am working with some of them to bring them to India," he added.He said 'S' in the TRUST acronym stands for 'Speak', urging both sides to communicate candidly and openly flag any hurdles or difficulties they face.He said the final 'T' stood for 'Track', emphasising the need to monitor outcomes and urging the IACC to hold both sides accountable.India needs about $430 billion in goods and services exports between Nov and March to meet its $1 trillion target for 2026-27, Goyal said, adding that India will have preferential trade access to $85 trillion of global GDP by next year, up from $70 trillion at present, as ongoing trade negotiations add another $15 trillion.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Asia’s stock markets dive as Anthropic debut fails to allay AI bubble fears
articles.summary: Indexes in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong fall amid tech sell-off.
articles.body:
Asian stock markets have opened to steep losses as fears that the AI boom is unsustainable continue to weigh on sentiment despite Anthropic’s blockbuster debut.

Markets in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong fell sharply on Friday, as investor excitement around the AI giant’s public listing failed to ally concerns about the sustainability of the multi-trillion-dollar investments propping up the sector.

Tokyo’s benchmark Nikkei 225 and Seoul’s Kospi each tumbled about 4.5 percent in morning trading, while the Taiex in Taipei plunged nearly 6 percent.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index dipped as much as 2 percent.

The sell-off reflects concerns that AI-led growth is slowing down and the “peak growth phase” may have already passed, said Rajat Agarwal, an Asia equity strategist with Societe Generale.

“The second element is on the demand vacuum that we are seeing,” Agarwal told Al Jazeera.

“At the time when foreigners are not buying, it is to be seen how long can the domestic investors stay put, particularly in Korea, on which the drawdown has been more severe.”

The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, even as Anthropic shares jumped 17 percent on their first day of trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange in New York.

Anthrophic’s stock price rose as high as $111 before settling just about $97, vaulting the Claude creator into the ranks of the world’s most valuable companies.

The San Francisco-based AI giant’s market debut came after it raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history , leapfrogging the previous record of $75bn set by SpaceX in June.

Despite the excitement around Anthrophic, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.3 percent, while the broader S&P500 fell 2 percent

Like Wall Street, Asia’s main bourses are heavily exposed to AI.

The region is home to some of the key players in the global AI ecosystem, including South Korean memory chip makers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, Taiwanese contract chipmaker TSMC, and Japanese investment holding company Softbank Group.

Tech firms have poured trillions of dollars into AI in recent year, stoking concern about the possibility of a speculative market bubble similar to the one that preceded the 2000 dot-com crash.

Global AI-related investment is projected to reach $2.7 trillion in 2026 and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner.
